title: A “slice of heaven”: The Cosplaying of Rural Life with #Homestead Tradwives in Appalachia
abstract: Abstract This article examines the intersection of the #Tradwife/#Homestead movements on social media within an Appalachian context. Utilizing ethonographic techniques that are designed to study the behavior and activities of online communities, the #Tradwife/#Homestead movements are explored using critical discourse analysis tools to examine issues related to class. gender/identity, and race. These reveal how Tradwife content creators in Appalachia may be contributing to dominant narratives relating to the region.

title: Butched Embodiment: Working Bodies and the Appalachian Landscape
abstract: Abstract In this essay, I posit that many rural and Appalachian women engage in a queer gender embodiment informed by manual labor and working-class experience—working the land in particular—which I call “butched embodiment.” I utilize both polished and raw forms of theorizing, in the way of academic texts from queer studies scholars and stories from rural America, with an emphasis on Appalachia and the South. Butched gender embodiment is a gender embodiment made “butch” not through personal identification, nor as an indication of one's sexuality, but as an embodiment that is ascribed the quality of “butchness” when viewed through an urban lens. The women in the narratives live in a culture that holds an alternative formulation of gender—one that, I argue, troubles even seemingly expansive models of gender embodiment utilized in queer studies. Through recognizing butched embodiment, we can better understand the metronormative and neoliberal undercurrent of discourse on queer experience—discourse that shapes local and global policy and that serves the US Empire. title: From the Editors
“What Makes an Appalachian?”: An Intersectional Psychological Investigation of Appalachian Identity and Protective Factors
abstract: Abstract The purpose of the current study was to apply an intersectional and strengths-based perspective to understand who endorses an Appalachian identity. Specifically, we explored the relationships among Appalachian identity endorsement, race and ethnicity endorsement, and positive childhood experiences (PCEs). We utilized intersectional techniques suggesting that psychologists should consider that (1) participants are multidimensional, (2) participants’ social group memberships are dynamic, (3) power is a feature of participant's intersectional positions, and (4) participants’ intersectional positions create outcomes of systemic advantage and disadvantage. Our exploratory analysis revealed two key factors related to Appalachian identity. First, those who are white are approximately 5.4 times more likely to self-identify as Appalachian. Individuals who already hold a marginalized or stereotyped social identity may be reluctant to self-identify as Appalachian, due to the stereotypes attributed to Appalachians. The Madison Women: Gender, Higher Education, and Literacy in Nineteenth-Century Appalachia
Gladys and Margaret Dysart, a Silhouette: “Well, then just leave it alone”
abstract: Abstract In this research note, I use portraiture methodology to explore the unsung environmental activism of Gladys Dysart McGaughy and Margaret Dysart in rural Appalachia during the early 1960s. Their story, centered on Dysart Woods, in Belmont County, Ohio, is being reconstructed through archival materials available thanks to three generations of community stewardship. This research note outlines the emerging portrait, drawing from three primary archives related to Dysart Woods (the Bartels Family private archive, the Captina Conservancy archive, and the Ohio University archive), as well as regional archives at the Belmont County District Library and the Ohio County Public Library. My emerging findings suggest that the Dysart family's stewardship reflects a broader legacy of female activism concerning the woods and demonstrates a strong sense of social responsibility akin to rural environmentalism. The depictions of Gladys and Margaret as well as Dysart Woods are called “silhouettes” throughout this research note, representing the initial stages of a forthcoming more comprehensive portrayal.

title: Holla! : Black Girlhood Pedagogies in an Abolitionist Appalachian Classroom
abstract: Abstract Black Girlhood Studies spotlights the oft-neglected intersection of gender, race, age, and place within feminist scholarship. These teaching notes reflect on the geopolitical landscape that informed the creation of our course on Black Girlhood Studies as Black Feminist Theory. We share how we and student scholars co-created our very own “holler,” a Black feminist abolitionist Appalachian classroom and pedagogical space, rooted in safety and care and the centering of Black girlhood knowledge and experiences. We share how young Black women college students were able to “holla back” and defy normative conceptions of gender, intersectionality, and activism in Appalachia. We offer interventions to free feminist pedagogical practice from its uncritical adultification of Black girlhood in the region's colleges and universities. We argue that embracing Black Girlhood Studies pedagogy bolsters students’ critical consciousness and resists the very sociopolitical contexts that wrongly dismiss Black girls as having little to contribute to feminist theories and praxes.

title: The Foxfire Book of Appalachian Women: Stories of Landscape and Community in the Mountain South
Guided by Starlight: Story Constellations of Queer Women's Resistance in Southern Appalachia
abstract: Abstract Queer women in Appalachia navigate a unique intersection of regional, gender, and sexuality-based identities, yet their stories of resilience and resistance are often overlooked in discussions of place and identity. This study centers on queer women who choose to remain in Appalachia for their university education rather than migrating to areas with more affirming cultural climates. Understanding why they stay—and how they resist societal pressures to leave—sheds light on the powerful ties between identity, geography, and resistance in a region often stereotyped as hostile to queer individuals. Using a “story constellation” approach informed by critical feminist lenses, this research explores the lived experiences of nine queer women attending universities located throughout Southern Appalachia. Participants shared stories of times they felt their identities affirmed, celebrated, and resisted on their college campuses, providing multidimensional views of how identity, place, and culture intersect for each woman. title: Hillbilly Highway: The Transappalachian Migration and the Making of a White Working Class
Ritual Remembrance: Folklore and Visionary Ideals
abstract: Abstract Cultural institutions house and categorize material culture, preserving the visionary ideals of the collecting institution through the choices and intention evident in collecting practices. Studying the collection through the lens of diverse representation reveals areas of erasure for marginalized voices within the historical narrative. A folkloristic practice that centers intersectional Appalachian identities is able to locate shared cultural markers and historical practices that resonate as true expressions of ancestral identity. At the Reece Museum, material culture collection and study include ancestral knowledge in a practice of ritual remembrance, which is explored within this article as a conceptual approach to museum work.

title: Lead Concentrations in Human, Cow's, and Goat's Milk in Rural Appalachia
abstract: Abstract Lead is neurotoxic particularly for the developing infant brain, and lead exposure should therefore be limited from environmental and nutritional sources. This study examined the lead concentrations of human, cow's, and goat's milk samples from Appalachia and compared them to the safety limits set by the World Health Organization. Twenty breastfeeding women residing in Appalachian Ohio provided human milk samples, while samples of cows’ and goats’ milk from local dairies were collected. The milks were analyzed for lead concentrations using inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS). Factors examined included maternal residential location, age of residence, water source, workplace exposure, smoking exposure, and sociodemographic characteristics. Overall, the milk samples’ lead levels were within the safety limits set by the WHO, and human milk lead levels were comparable to locally sourced cow's and goat's milk. Significant factors associated with higher lead levels in human milk samples were older houses (p = 0.001) and the number of years living in the house (p = 0.013). title: Domestic Life Amidst a Logging Economy in Menifee County, Kentucky
abstract: Abstract This research note provides a summary of archival, oral historical, and archaeological investigations into two early twentieth-century domestic sites situated along the East Fort of Indian Creek in Menifee County, Kentucky. The occupants participated in farming, trapping, and especially in the harvesting of timber. Archaeology provides a glimpse into the material culture in use at the sites, and the family histories showcase the wide range of local adaptations to the logging economy.

title: Breaking Beans
Representation and Resistance: Identity Expression in Podcasts from Appalachia
abstract: Abstract This study considers the way podcasters who produce shows about Appalachia use the medium to express ideas about social identity and challenge negative stereotypes about the region. In sixteen qualitative interviews, podcasters expressed a desire to combat regional essentialism by amplifying voices and complicating existing narratives of Appalachia as a cultural monolith. Participants hoped to develop project identity to pursue the goals of encouraging regional connection and deconstructing Appalachian stereotypes. Participants also described at times competing interests in combating those stereotypes while also avoiding essentialism that might lead them to generalization themselves.

Introduction: Beyond Hollow Materialism
abstract: Abstract This introduction to the special issue, “Transformative Approaches to Materiality in Appalachian Studies,” provides theoretical background and examples that demonstrate applications of new material culture and materiality theory to key Appalachian studies themes. It offers new directions for the study of material entanglement in social relationships by reviewing the history of material culture studies in the Appalachian context, fundamental theoretical propositions emerging from the “material turn” in social theory, and examples drawn from ethnographic and archaeological research into the patterns of use of material culture in the timber country of West Virginia and coalfields of eastern Kentucky. Finally, this introduction summarizes key questions offered by the contributors and invites further discourse amongst scholars of Appalachia about the role of material culture and materiality in shaping our research and engaged practices.

title: From the Editors
We Are What We Consume
abstract: Abstract This illustrated article explores how the plastic cycle connects Appalachia to the rest of the nation. I write from my personal experience living, working, and playing in the New River watershed, which feeds the Ohio River. These experiences led me to explore connections between fossil fuel production, microplastic pollution, and the work of artists and activists working to support sustainable solutions for our region and our planet. Through photographs and text, I explore an arts-based response to protect the region's water resources and explain how the cultural resources of the region can be used to protect our most valuable resource—fresh water.

Domestic Orientalism: Barbara Kingsolver's Demon Copperhead as a Counter to the Stereotyping of the Appalachians
abstract: Abstract Barbara Kingsolver's Pulitzer Prize-winning 2022 novel Demon Copperhead deals directly with the impact of the opioid crisis on life in Lee County, in the Appalachian region of Virginia. Demon Copperhead is a coming-of-age story that traces the experiences of its eponymous narrator/protagonist from his birth until adulthood as he grows up in Lee County. In a literary sense, this personal story is complicated by the fact that Kingsolver's novel is also a carefully crafted retelling of Charles Dickens's 1850 novel David Copperfield. Kingsolver's story is deeply rooted in its historical moment, focusing on the opioid crisis that began in the 1990s and continued to worsen through the first decades of the twenty-first century, especially in rural areas such as Lee County. Kingsolver's detailed, sympathetic portrayal of Appalachian culture also deals with broader issues, addressing the common tendency in American culture to depict the people of the Appalachians in stereotypical ways that assume the backwardness and even depravity of the “rednecks” and “hillbillies” who inhabit the area. title: Doors Unmarked: A Study of Custodial Professionalism in Photos
abstract: Abstract Blue-collar and manual labor is typified as unskilled and is, overall, devalued in American culture. I argue that workers in these careers are made socially “invisible” in popular culture based on the work they perform. I find that custodians are, in fact, professionals, and through their ability to perform their work with expertise and care, they also perform a unique type of customer service for their “customers.” Further, custodians also create strong professional networks for themselves while on the job. These networks serve as a vital support system, both professionally and personally. My study includes custodians who work at a large state university in Appalachia, with visual data in photographs. I expand my analysis of these workers to make connections to manual labor in general, in the United States.

title: The Archaeology of Multigenerational Social Reproduction: Economic Strategies and Material Life at the Gibbs Farm
abstract: Abstract The Gibbs farm in East Tennessee near Knoxville was operated between the 1790s and the early twentieth century. Historical details related to the farm appear to illustrate a typical middle-class Southern Appalachian farm. Upon closer scrutiny, the economic practices and material life at the farm illustrate how the Gibbs family effectively sustained four generations for over a century. As an example of social reproduction, aggressive commercial farming and related inheritance practices allowed family members to gift farmland and dowries to adult children. Material culture at the farm, such as a log dwelling, a pork diet, and use of inexpensive redware, likewise illustrates a success vs. excess material standard. Family members lived comfortably, drew upon familiar vernacular material traditions, and were active commercial consumers, yet overall chose to live conservatively and invest resources back into the means of production. Accepted uncritically, economically conservative practices and use of folk material items could be construed as reinforcing typical negative cultural tropes projected upon the region.

title: Reading, Writing, and Queer Survival: Affects, Matterings, and Literacies Across Appalachia
No Son of Mine: A Memoir
Language, Material Culture, and Materiality in Appalachia
abstract: Abstract This article focuses on excerpts from interviews conducted with Appalachian speakers between 1999 and 2008 in the Blue Ridge Mountains of western North Carolina, examining the role played by objects in the construction of identity within interview interactions. Normally, as a sociolinguist, my research focuses on language use although more recently, I have considered material culture and its role in social meaning-making as well, combining considerations of linguistic and physical artifacts. This paper will extend such analysis, pulling in ideas of community and place—and family—into a discussion of the interaction of language and material culture in the (re-)creation of an “Appalachian” identity and history.

title: “Moving to Mecca”—A Case Study of Language Ideology, Insecurity, and the Uprooting of Appalachian Englishes
abstract: Abstract This paper, through a case study of a middle-aged university administrator, investigates how mobile Appalachians—those who uproot themselves from Appalachia and move for professional or personal reasons—navigate linguistic insecurity. Appalachian college students are often discriminated against via codes of power that reify standard language ideologies. Through a quantitative analysis, we argue that Appalachian Kentuckians are more likely to change the way they speak as a product of linguistic insecurity compared to Kentuckians from other parts of the state. Through a qualitative narrative analysis, we see how one participant, Zoey, responded to an inciting incident of linguistic insecurity that propelled her to change the way that she speaks—a phenomenon we term uprootedness. We then explore how she negotiates this change later in life while working in a professional university setting. We provide preliminary evidence that the linguistic discrimination mobile Appalachians experience in college years can carry forward into their professional lives. title: Funerary Photographs as Enduring Kinship and Community Ties in Twentieth-Century Appalachia and Transappalachia: Material and Relational Methods
abstract: Abstract This research note proposes a relational methodology for examining the production and exchange of funerary photographs in which family and community members posed with the deceased in early twentieth-century Appalachia, and for exploring how this practice expanded through the mid-twentieth century between Appalachian diasporic communities in the industrial Midwest and their family members who remained “at home.” Initially associated with the Victorian period across European and Anglo-American contexts, these photographs evolved to serve crucial social functions in maintaining community ties across geographic distances. This research examines how the materiality and relational properties of these ritual objects were central to their exchange between families separated by economic migration. I draw on the suggestion of Elizabeth Edwards and Janice Hart to understand photographs as active objects rather than valuing them solely for image content, as well as Marilyn Strathern's work on relationality, which demonstrates that material objects actively constitute rather than merely reflect social relationships.

title: Reporting on Dental Health in Appalachia: A Critical Discourse Analysis of Newsprint Media Among National and Regional Outlets
abstract: Abstract This study employs critical discourse analysis to examine newsprint media representations of dental health in Appalachia from 2000 to 2022, focusing on The New York Times, Pittsburgh Post-Gazette, and The Herald-Dispatch. Utilizing Teun van Dijk's discursive strategies, the analysis reveals how national and regional outlets perpetuate stereotypes and systemic biases by emphasizing personal responsibility, poverty, and addiction over structural barriers like limited access to dental care. Key themes include drug use, lack of medical care, environmental issues, policy, and a “culture of poverty,” with strategies such as hyperbole, humanitarianism, and distancing reinforcing status quo ideologies. The findings highlight the media's role in shaping public perceptions of Appalachian dental health, underscoring the need for more nuanced reporting to address systemic inequities and inform effective public health interventions in the region.
